samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
If I could start anywhere, I would start not at the beginning but in the middle of a morning that hasn't quite decided what it wants to be. The light is coming sideways through a window, thin and gold, catching dust that I never notice at noon. There is a cup of tea going cold because I keep getting distracted by the sound of birds outside, and a book face-down on the table, holding my place with its spine. Nothing important is happening. And for some reason, that feels like the most honest place to begin, because most of life is not made of beginnings or endings at all. It is made of these middles, these unremarkable stretches where we are waiting for water to boil or for a thought to finish forming, and in that waiting we become ourselves without noticing.

I have always been a walker. Not a hiker, exactly, not someone with poles and summits and photographs at the top, but a walker of streets and shorelines and supermarket aisles when it is raining too hard to be outside. Walking does something to thought that sitting still cannot do. At a desk, my mind goes in circles, neat and anxious. On foot, it goes in spirals. It loosens. A problem that felt like a wall at nine in the morning becomes, by the third mile, a wall with a gate in it somewhere, if I keep going long enough to find it. The old philosophers knew this. So did poets, and grandmothers who said go get some fresh air as if air could be medicine. They were right. The body moving at three miles an hour is the right speed for the mind to keep up with itself, not so fast that it panics, not so slow that it sleeps.

There is a particular walk I return to in memory even when I am thousands of miles away from it. It goes past a row of houses where someone always seems to be cooking onions, down a hill that makes my knees complain, along a river that is brown in winter and green in summer, and then up through a small wood where the ground is soft with last year's leaves. I have walked it in grief and in love and in boredom. I have walked it talking aloud to myself, rehearsing apologies and job interviews and imaginary arguments I would never actually have. I have walked it with other people and learned that you can say things side by side that you could never say face to face. There is mercy in not having to look at someone while you tell them the truth. The path holds the silences for you. The trees do not rush to fill them.

Libraries taught me another kind of walking. As a child I thought a library was a quiet place, and it is, but only on the surface. Underneath, it is the loudest place in the world. Every shelf is shouting, not rudely, but insistently: take me, try me, I contain multitudes, I contain recipes for soup and histories of empires that fell because of bad weather and love poems written by people who died before electricity. I used to wander the stacks with no plan at all, pulling out books because I liked the color of the spine or the strangeness of a title. That is how I found most of the books that mattered to me. Not through recommendations. Through accidents. Through serendipity, which is a beautiful word for letting the world arrange your education while you pretend you are just browsing.

I wonder sometimes what we lose when everything is searchable. When an algorithm knows what I liked last Tuesday and feeds me more of the same on Wednesday, I become more efficiently myself, but a narrower version. The library never did that. The library put books about beekeeping next to books about medieval theology because the alphabet is a strange and democratic organizer, and in that forced adjacency my brain made leaps it would never have made on its own. I think we need more alphabetical accidents in life. We need to be shelved next to people and ideas that do not match our preferences. We need browsing, in the old sense — slow, inefficient, hands touching actual paper, eyes drifting.

And paper itself. I love the smell of old books, that vanilla and dust and faintly sweet decay. I love marginalia left by strangers: underlined sentences, a question mark in pencil, once, gloriously, a dried flower pressed between pages 112 and 113 of a book of poems. Who left it? Was it a bookmark in a hurry, or a deliberate offering? Did they finish the book? Did they love the person who gave them the flower, or were they trying to forget them by flattening the evidence? A book is never just a book. It is a record of all the hands that have held it. Even now, with screens glowing everywhere, I think we are hungry for that kind of tactile history. We want to know that other people have been here before us, turning the same pages, stuck on the same paragraph.

The sea does the same thing on a larger scale. Stand at the edge of any ocean and you are immediately corrected in your sense of importance. It does not care about your deadlines. It was pulling back and pushing forward long before language, and it will continue after. But it is not cruel about it. It is indifferent in a way that feels like relief. I have gone to the sea when I did not know what else to do with sadness, and I have never asked it to fix anything. I have just watched waves do their repetitive, unoriginal, perfect work, and my breathing has slowed to match them without my permission. Scientists can explain tides and moons and gravity, and they are right, but they are not complete. The sea also explains that most things return, altered. That erosion is slow but real. That you can be both powerful and unable to hold onto anything. Every wave is an argument for letting go gracefully.

My grandmother never talked about the sea that way. She talked about practical things at her kitchen table, which was where all important philosophy happened in our family. She made bread with hands that knew measurements by feel. A little more flour because it is humid today. A little less salt because your grandfather's blood pressure. She taught me that knowledge lives in the body, not just in books. You can read about kneading for a hundred pages and still do it wrong until someone puts their hands over yours and says, like this, softer, you're fighting it. There is a whole epistemology in that sentence. How many things in life get worse because we fight them? Grief, dough, insomnia, other people. Softness is not weakness. It is technique.

I still try to make that bread sometimes, and mine is never quite as good. That is partly flour and partly impatience. Bread does not care about your schedule. It rises in its own time. You can coax it with warmth, but you cannot command it. I find this both infuriating and instructive. We live in a culture that has declared waiting a design failure. We buffer, we preload, we pay extra for same-day delivery of things we did not know we wanted yesterday. Bread laughs at that. So do gardens. So do children, and healing, and learning a language, and falling out of love. The most important processes have an internal clock that does not synchronize with our phones. If we had any wisdom, we would build more of our lives around that fact instead of constantly trying to hack our way past it.

Languages, since I mentioned them. I am fascinated by the words other languages have that mine does not. The Portuguese saudade, a longing for something absent, perhaps something that never existed. The Danish hygge, which we have tried to import and sell as candles, but which is really about shelter from the world with people you trust. The Japanese concept of wabi-sabi, beauty in imperfection and impermanence, the cracked cup more lovely for having been mended. Each of these words is a small window. They prove that your mother tongue is not a complete description of being human. It is just the house you grew up in. Other people grew up in other houses, with different windows facing different weather. Learning even a fragment of another language is like visiting. You realize the furniture could be arranged differently. You realize your own home, beloved as it is, is not the only way to live indoors.

And yet language fails us constantly, which is also beautiful. Every day we say "I'm fine" when we are twelve different things, none of them fine. We say "soon" and mean hours or months depending on our culture and our hope. We try to describe the exact color of a sunset to someone who wasn't there and we resort to food words — peach, honey, apricot — because color alone is not enough, we need taste. Poets spend their lives trying to close the gap between experience and words, and they fail gloriously, and the failure creates something new. Maybe that is the point. Language is not a bucket to carry meaning without spilling. It is a net. Most of the water runs through. What stays caught glitters enough that we keep casting it.

Memory has the same holes. I used to think forgetting was a defect, a kind of mental moth eating the fabric. Now I am not so sure. Imagine remembering everything: every embarrassing thing said in seventh grade, every license plate, every pain in perfect detail. We would be crushed under the archive. Forgetting is editing. It is mercy. But it is also terrifying, because it edits without asking permission. I can remember the exact pattern of the wallpaper in a house I left when I was six, but I cannot reliably remember why I walked into this room just now. I can sing advertising jingles from thirty years ago while names of people I met last week evaporate on contact. The mind keeps what it thinks is useful, and it is often wrong about usefulness. That is why we write things down. That is why we tell stories at kitchen tables, repeating them until the family version becomes smoother and funnier and less true than what happened, but truer in another way — it becomes the story of who we think we are.

Stories. I could stay there forever. A story is how we smuggle meaning past the guards. Tell someone a list of facts about loneliness and they will nod politely. Tell them about an old man who sets two plates every night for a wife who has been dead for five years, not because he forgets, but because the single plate makes the table look wrong, and they will feel it in their ribs. We are not rational creatures who sometimes tell stories. We are storytelling creatures who sometimes manage to be rational. That order matters. It explains politics and religion and why arguments about data rarely change anybody's mind unless there is a story underneath for the data to ride on.

At night, when the day's noise has thinned, I often think about scale. Astronomers tell us the observable universe is about ninety-three billion light years across, and that there are more stars than grains of sand on all Earth's beaches, a sentence that has been repeated so often it has become smooth, but if you actually try to feel it, it tilts the mind. I go outside on clear nights far from the city and look up and try not to reach for my phone to name the constellations. I try to let them be unnamed for a while, just points and patterns my ancestors saw and feared and navigated by. It makes my problems smaller without making them unimportant. A kind of perspective that does not dismiss. Yes, my anxiety is real. Yes, it is also occurring on a small rock orbiting an ordinary star in an unremarkable corner of a galaxy that is itself one of billions. Both truths can hold at once. In fact, they must. If we hold only the first, we drown. If we hold only the second, we become cold.

I have similar double thoughts about technology. I am grateful for it and tired of it, often in the same hour. I love that I can hear the voice of a friend on another continent as if she is in the next room. I love that a question at midnight can be answered by an archive larger than any library I will ever walk in. And I hate the way a screen makes every moment feel slightly insufficient, as if real life were the draft and the posted version were the final. I hate how attention — which is really just love in its daily form, noticing — gets chopped into fragments and sold. I am trying, in small rebellions, to reclaim it. Leaving the phone in another room while I eat. Reading one thing all the way to the end. Watching rain without filming it. These are not grand gestures. They are maintenance. You do not reclaim a garden in a day. You weed. You water. You repeat.

Friendship, when it is good, is also maintenance. The great friendships of my life have not survived because of intensity but because of regularity. The text that says thinking of you, no reply needed. The walk that happens every Thursday even when neither person has interesting news. The friend who remembers that your mother has a hospital appointment and asks the next day how it went. In our youth we think friendship is about being fascinating. In middle age we learn it is about being present. Presence is rarer. Anyone can be fascinating for an evening. To be present for a decade, through job losses and babies and boring stretches and the long slow care of aging parents — that is an art form. I have failed at it, sometimes. I have been the friend who meant to call. Intentions do not keep people warm. Actions do. I am still learning.

Letters helped, once. I mean real letters, paper in envelopes, stamps licked, handwriting that slanted when the writer was tired. A letter had a built-in delay that gave it dignity. You wrote what mattered because you could not easily take it back or add a second thought thirty seconds later. You lived with your sentences. And receiving one: the recognition of handwriting on an envelope could make a whole day change color. I still keep a box of them, tied with nothing fancier than a rubber band that has lost its elasticity. I rarely reread them. That is not the point. The point is that they exist, physical proof that at certain moments, someone sat down and thought of me for longer than a notification. I wonder what will be in the boxes of the future. Screenshots? Printouts of threads? Maybe sentiment will find new containers. It usually does. Humans are incorrigibly sentimental under all our irony.

Irony itself. We wear a lot of it now, as armor. It is safer to make a joke about caring than to care sincerely and be seen doing it. Sincerity is vulnerable. It can be mocked. But I find myself craving sincerity more as I get older, not less. Say the kind thing plainly. Admit you were moved by a song with embarrassing lyrics. Tell people you love them in sentences that are not camouflaged. The world has enough cleverness. Cleverness is cheap and abundant and often just cruelty with better vocabulary. Kindness requires more imagination, because you have to picture a life not your own. I want to be better at that kind of imagination. I want to practice it until it becomes reflex.

There is also the question of making things. Not necessarily art with a capital A, though that counts. Making soup. Making a shelf that is almost level. Making a playlist for someone who is sad. We are, I think, wired to leave small evidence that we passed through the world and rearranged a tiny part of it on purpose. A child stacking stones understands this. An adult who has been beaten down by systems that treat them as consumers first and creators second may forget. But the urge returns in strange places — in lockdown gardens, in sourdough starters given names like pets, in knitted scarves that are slightly uneven. The unevenness is the signature. A machine can make it perfect. Only a person can make it slightly wrong in an interesting way.

Time, of course, keeps making us slightly wrong and interesting too. In my twenties, time felt like an endless corridor. In my forties, it feels more like a house I have lived in long enough to notice the light changing earlier in the autumn. I do not fear aging in the way I expected to. I fear wasting it, which is different. I fear spending too many evenings scrolling through the lives of strangers while my own life, unphotographed, goes by in the next room asking to be lived. I fear becoming brittle — of opinion, of habit, of heart. So I try to stay teachable. I try to be the oldest person in a class sometimes, fumbling with a new skill, reminded that incompetence is not humiliation, it is the entry fee. Everyone who is good at anything paid it once.

And what about solitude, which is not the same as loneliness, though they share a border and often cross it without a passport? I need solitude the way I need sleep. Without it I become a lesser version, reactive, noisy inside. A few hours alone with a book or a path or even a sink full of dishes and warm water resets something. Loneliness, on the other hand, is solitude with the door locked from the outside. It aches. We have built a world that gives people more ways to contact each other and, paradoxically, more ways to feel unseen. The cure, insofar as there is one, seems stubbornly analog: shared meals, shared work, neighborhoods where people know each other's names and dogs. Small, repeatable belonging. Not followers. Neighbors.

If I sound like I am wandering, I am. That was the promise when I sat down, not to march in a straight line to a conclusion, but to wander honestly and see what turns up. A straight line is efficient, but life has never been efficient for me. It has been more like that walk I described: past the onions, down the hill, along the changing river. Sometimes I have gotten lost. Once, literally, in a foreign city where my phone died and the street signs were in a script I could not read, and I had to navigate by following a river and asking directions with gestures and a phrasebook's desperate smile. I remember that evening more fondly than most perfectly planned days. Being lost forced me to look up. Most of the time, I am looking down, at a screen, at my feet, at my to-do list. Getting lost, occasionally, is a correction.

There are other corrections. Illness is one, and grief, those brutal teachers no one enrolls with voluntarily. They strip away the decorative parts of a personality and show what remains. I have seen people become, in suffering, not bitter, but clarified. I have also seen people become bitter, and I do not judge them; pain does not ennoble automatically, it just exposes. The work is in what we do after exposure. Do we build scar tissue or do we build bridges? Sometimes, honestly, we build walls and need them for a while. Healing is not linear, another sentence that has become a poster, but stays true no matter how many mugs it is printed on. Some days you are fine. Some days a song in a grocery store undoes you between the cereal and the milk. Both days belong to the same life.

Perhaps, in the end — and I am not at the end, I am in the middle again, which is where I started — what I want most is to pay better attention. To the light sideways through the window. To the friend telling a story I have heard before, because the telling matters more than the novelty. To the taste of tea even when it has gone a bit cold. Attention is a form of prayer for people who are not sure what they pray to. It says: this moment is not a rehearsal. This is the thing itself. Mary Oliver asked what we plan to do with our one wild and precious life, and that question used to terrify me because I thought it required a grand answer. A mission. A legacy. Now I think the answer might be small and daily. I plan to notice. I plan to make bread badly and share it anyway. I plan to walk, and read, and write letters I may deliver by hand. I plan to be shelved, now and then, next to the unexpected.

And when I fail — because I will, regularly, spectacularly — I plan to begin again in the middle. Tomorrow morning will have its own sideways light. There will be more dust, more birds, more books face-down holding my place. The river will be green or brown depending on the season. The sea, wherever it is, will be doing its repetitive work without needing my witness, but I will go witness it anyway when I can, because witnessing changes the witness. That is the whole beautiful loop. We attend to the world, and in attending, we are remade. Word by word, walk by walk, loaf by uneven loaf.

So I will keep going. Not because I have reached a conclusion, but because stopping here would be a lie about how thinking actually works. Thought doesn't conclude. It pauses. It puts a bookmark in, sometimes a dried flower, and closes the cover for the night. In the morning, if we are lucky, we open it again to find that the page we left looks different, because we are different, even slightly, even by one night's sleep and dreams we don't remember. That difference, tiny and cumulative, is a whole life. I am grateful for it. I am curious about it. And for now, that curiosity is enough to stand up, rinse the cold tea from the cup, lace my shoes, and head out the door to see what the path is doing today.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I am thinking, for no particular reason, about a kitchen at three in the morning.

Not a dramatic kitchen. Not the scene of a revelation or a disaster. Just a small room with a refrigerator humming a little too loudly, a chipped blue mug on the counter, and that particular quality of light that comes from a streetlamp outside the window mixing with the pale glow above the stove. At three in the morning, ordinary objects stop performing their daytime roles. The chairs are not for sitting. The table is not for eating. They are just shapes that have agreed, temporarily, to be still. And the person standing there in socks, opening the refrigerator and forgetting why, is not really looking for food. They are looking for a reason to be awake in a world that is mostly asleep, and for proof that the house will remember how to be a house again when morning comes.

I think we spend most of our lives in that three-a.m. kitchen, metaphorically speaking. We stand between one completed thing and the next not-yet-begun thing, holding a glass of water, listening to the building settle. The grand narratives we tell ourselves — career, love, ambition, legacy — they work fine in daylight. At night they loosen. What remains are smaller truths: I am thirsty. I am a little lonely. The floor is cold. Tomorrow I should call my sister. I never learned how to fold a fitted sheet properly and probably never will. These are not lesser truths. They might be the only ones that never lie to us.

My grandmother kept buttons in a biscuit tin.

It was a round tin, once red, with a picture of a Scottish landscape faded to a kind of optimistic grey. Inside were hundreds of buttons that belonged to no living garment: pearl buttons, wooden toggles, brass uniform buttons, tiny shirt buttons so white they seemed to glow, one enormous Bakelite button that must have come from a coat worn by a giant in a story. Whenever a button fell off anything in her house, it went into the tin, not with any real expectation of reunion, but with the faith that separation should not mean disappearance. As a child I would pour them onto the carpet and sort them by color, then by size, then by imagined importance. The tin smelled faintly of metal and shortbread and old houses.

She is gone now, and I do not know where the tin went. Someone probably threw it away during the necessary cruelty of clearing a home. That is what we do. We stand in rooms full of a life and we ask, ruthlessly, what is useful, what is valuable, what can be kept in a smaller flat, what will anyone actually want. And a tin of orphaned buttons fails every test except the only one that mattered to her, which was: did someone once need this, and might they again?

I think about that tin more often than I think about many supposedly important things. I think we all have a version of it, even if ours is a drawer full of cables for phones we no longer own, or a phone full of photographs we never look at, or a mind full of faces from a school corridor thirty years ago whose names arrive in the shower without warning. We are collectors of loose buttons. We cannot help it. Letting go completely would feel less like tidying and more like erasure. So we keep. We keep ticket stubs and recipes written in handwriting that slopes uphill, voicemails we cannot delete because the voice in them no longer exists anywhere else. We keep because memory is an unreliable tenant and objects are its rent receipts.

Not far from where I imagine that kitchen, there is a sea. There is always a sea somewhere in my thinking, even when I am inland, even when the nearest coast is hours away. The sea is the original three-a.m. kitchen: restless, repetitive, indifferent, and strangely comforting because of its indifference. It does not need you to understand it. It was doing this before you arrived and it will continue after you have gone home with sand in your shoes.

I love the hour when people leave the beach. Early evening, the lifeguards packing up, families shaking out towels, children protesting with the full force of their lungs as if being taken away from the water were a historical injustice. Then quiet. The sea gets its room back. The waves seem louder not because they have changed but because we have stopped competing with them. I have stood on shorelines in that hour and felt the specific relief of being unimportant in a beautiful place. The universe is not sending me a message. The tide is not a metaphor unless I need it to be. It is just water obeying the moon, which is miracle enough without my decorating it.

And yet we decorate. We must. A fisherman sees weather. A child sees a monster’s bathtub. A poet sees grief with better rhythm. A geologist sees time turned liquid. All of them are right, which is another way of saying the sea is large enough to contain our projections without being reduced by them. I wish more things in life were like that. I wish opinions and memories and other people could receive what we pour into them and remain themselves. Perhaps they do, and we are only too impatient to notice.

If the sea is where I go to feel small in a good way, the library is where I go to feel less alone in my smallness.

A good library has a smell that no architect can design and no cleaning product can erase: paper, dust warmed by radiators, wooden shelves, the faint sweetness of old glue. It is the smell of many minds having been somewhere before you. I love the democratic chaos of it. In one aisle, a teenager is cramming for an exam she is convinced will decide her entire future. Two shelves over, a retired man is reading a biography of a general he despises, very slowly, with a pencil. Somewhere a toddler is treating a picture book as both literature and percussion instrument. Nobody is asked to justify their presence. You do not need a ticket, a membership to the right club, or a convincing explanation. You need, mostly, curiosity, or at least the desire for a warm chair and other people being quiet nearby.

Books have often been described as conversations with the dead, which is true but incomplete. They are also arguments with the living who are not in the room, rehearsals for lives we will never lead, and instructions left by strangers who assumed, generously, that we might show up one day needing to know how to fix a bicycle, identify a mushroom, or survive heartbreak in nineteenth-century Russia. Every library card is a small act of optimism: I believe I will return. I believe returning is possible. I believe the future version of me will still want to know things.

I sometimes imagine all the marginalia ever written — the underlinings, the exclamation marks, the furious little “no!” in a margin from 1974 — rising off the pages at night after closing, and having a meeting. What a parliament that would be. The romantics would sigh too loudly. The scientists would demand evidence. Some anonymous reader from Ohio who wrote “this happened to me” beside a paragraph and nothing else would bring the whole room to silence, because that is the entire history of reading in four words: this happened to me.

Between the sea and the library there is, inevitably, a walk through a city.

I am a devoted, inefficient walker. I take wrong turns with confidence. I stop to read plaques about people I have never heard of who did something admirable with water pressure in 1892. I look up at windows and invent the lives behind them with no evidence whatsoever: there, a violin teacher who is beloved and slightly feared; there, a couple who have just agreed, after a long discussion, to get a cat; there, a man eating toast alone and enjoying the solitude he pretends to complain about. Cities reward this kind of attention. They are collages pretending to be plans. A medieval lane leans against a glass tower; a bakery exhales into a bus stop; somebody has planted geraniums in a window box above a shop selling nothing you can identify, and the geraniums are thriving out of pure municipal stubbornness.

Walking also restores a proper relationship with time. In a car, distance is an inconvenience measured in minutes of delay. On a screen, the whole world is allegedly instant and therefore oddly weightless. On foot, a mile is a mile. It takes the time it takes, and during that time your thoughts are allowed to finish their sentences. Some of my best ideas have arrived at walking pace, not because walking is magic but because it bores the mind in the right way. The anxious, performative part of the brain gives up trying to be impressive and wanders off, and underneath it, quieter thoughts come out like animals at dusk. A solution to a letter I have been avoiding. The realization that I was wrong in an argument three weeks ago, in a specific way I can now name. The first line of something worth writing, which will, of course, have vanished by the time I find a pen, because the mind enjoys small cruelties.

If I walk long enough and in the right direction, I would like there to be a garden.

I am not a skilled gardener. My talents run toward hopeful planting and apologetic watering. But I love gardens precisely because they refuse to be hurried and refuse, also, to be fully controlled, which makes them honest teachers. You can prepare soil, you can read the packet, you can watch the forecast like a stockbroker, and still the slugs will hold their banquet and the one plant you neglected will produce an embarrassing abundance of flowers out of spite or joy. A garden is a collaboration with forces that have no interest in your self-esteem. Rain does not care that you had plans. Frost has not read your schedule. This is, after initial irritation, a relief.

There is a humility forced on anyone who has ever tried to grow tomatoes. The plant does not want your anxiety. It wants light, water, support, and to be left mostly alone to do the ancient work of turning sunlight into something red and improbable. People are not tomatoes — we require considerably more conversation and are worse at photosynthesizing compliments — but the lesson leaks across species. So many living things do not need us to hover. They need conditions, patience, and occasional intervention. Love, I suspect, is often gardening mistaken for architecture. We think we are building each other. More often we are just trying not to block the light.

Seeds, too, are an outrageous gamble that we perform casually. We put a dry, dead-looking speck into dirt and then act as though a green shoot is a reasonable expectation. It is not reasonable. It is a resurrection staged at windowsill scale, and we respond by saying, “Oh good, the basil’s up.” Humans are at their best, I think, when wonder becomes routine without becoming dull. The first time a child sees a sprout, they gasp correctly. The adult says, “Water it on Thursdays,” and in that sentence is the whole tragedy and triumph of growing up: we learn how to keep miracles alive by putting them in the calendar.

Somewhere between the garden and the library, language is growing wild.

I collect lost and endangered words the way my grandmother collected buttons. Did you know there is an old word, “apricity,” for the warmth of the sun in winter? That specific, stolen sweetness on your face in January while your hands are still cold in your pockets — someone treasured it enough to name it. There is “psithurism,” the sound of wind in trees. There is the Scots word “tartle,” for that panicked hesitation when you are about to introduce someone whose name you have forgotten. Everyone has tartled. Everyone has stood there with a smile bolted on, saying, “And this is...” while their brain ransacked burning archives. A language that has a word for that embarrassment is a language paying attention to real life.

Words disappear when the experiences they name become rare, or when we become too embarrassed to admit we still have the experiences. We lose words for kinds of snow when winters soften. We lose words for tools when the trades that used them fade. We gain others, of course — every generation coins bright slang that will embarrass it in photographs later — but each lost word is a small window painted shut. The feeling may still exist, wandering the house, but it has one fewer door to enter by.

That is why I write things down, I suppose. Not because my observations are uniquely valuable, but because notation is a form of hospitality. A sentence says: this moment was here, it can sit down. The bus driver who sang quietly to the radio at dawn. The way my friend laughs before she knows why she is laughing, as if her body got the joke first. The old man in the park feeding pigeons with the seriousness of a diplomat distributing aid. If no one writes them, do they vanish? Not entirely. The world is not so fragile. But our shared memory of the world becomes thinner, more reliant on headlines, and headlines were never designed to carry the weight of ordinary tenderness.

Ordinary tenderness is most visible, to me, among strangers.

I love trains for this reason. A train is a temporary village moving at speed, full of people who have agreed by unspoken treaty to be near each other without demanding anything. They share armrests and sighs and the announcement that the buffet car has, once again, a limited service. They witness each other’s small surrenders: the businessman asleep with his mouth open, suddenly eight years old; the student mouthing vocabulary; the woman knitting something that may become a sweater or may become a long, woolen intention. When the train stops unexpectedly between stations, a brief society forms. People make eye contact. Someone jokes. Someone shares a mint as if mints were now the local currency. Then we move again, and the society dissolves without sadness, having completed itself.

We are told, constantly, to fear strangers, and of course there are reasons, and of course caution is a form of intelligence. But a life organized entirely around suspicion becomes a very small room. Most strangers are not threats or angels; they are protagonists of stories we will never hear, carrying shopping and worries and a song stuck in their heads. The woman across the aisle is not “a passenger.” She is someone who once, at sixteen, cut her own hair and regretted it within the hour, who knows exactly how her mother takes tea, who may be traveling toward the hardest conversation of her year while highlighting a magazine article about houseplants. To imagine that, briefly and without intrusion, is not sentimentality. It is accuracy. Everyone is more specific than the role they occupy in our day.

At night, when the trains have stopped and the garden is dark and the library is locked, there are stars, performing their old trick of making time visible.

Astronomy is the rudest and kindest science. It tells you that the light entering your eye left its source before your civilization learned to write, before, perhaps, your species had a word for winter. It tells you that you are made of materials forged in ancient stellar violence, which means that “star stuff” is not a pretty line but a materials report. And then, having dismantled your importance with one hand, it gives you the night sky for free, every clear night, no ticket required, the original public library of light. Kind and rude. Like all the best teachers.

I find it helps to be regularly outscaled. Problems do not disappear under the stars — the rent is still due, the diagnosis is still pending, the apology still unsent — but they regain their actual size. My embarrassment at something I said in 2016 has survived years of feeding; under Orion it looks, correctly, like a very small animal I have been keeping as a pet. I can let it go. Or at least stop taking it for walks.

The universe is under no obligation to make us feel significant, and I have come to prefer it that way. Meaning that is handed to us cheaply tends to expire quickly. Meaning we assemble ourselves — from buttons and tides and other people’s handwriting, from gardens that partially fail, from walks and trains and three-a.m. glasses of water — is sturdier because we know what it cost to gather. It is a biscuit tin of a philosophy. None of the pieces match. All of them were once needed. Together they make a sound when you shake them, like a very small, private applause.

If I could send a letter to the future, it would not contain predictions. Predictions are just the present wearing a false moustache. I would send a list of things I hope still exist, and a confession of things I hope we have outgrown.

I hope there are still libraries where a person can be warm and unproductive in public without shame. I hope someone is still keeping a tin of useless, beautiful salvage. I hope children are taught the names of trees with the same seriousness as the names of brands, and that some adult, somewhere, still says “apricity” out loud on a cold bright morning and makes another person repeat it, delighted. I hope we still walk places slowly enough to invent the lives behind windows, and that we hold those inventions lightly, knowing the real lives are better. I hope strangers on stalled trains still share mints. I hope we have become braver about tenderness and more suspicious of cruelty dressed as realism. I hope we have learned that attention is not a passive act but a moral one: what we notice, we protect; what we ignore, we allow to be taken.

And I hope, in that future, someone stands in a kitchen at three in the morning, in socks, holding a glass of water for no clear reason, and feels — not happy, exactly, not solved — but accompanied. By the hum of the refrigerator. By the long human history of being awake when the world is quiet. By all the small salvaged moments rattling gently in the tin.

Morning will come, as it rudely and mercifully does. The chairs will become chairs again. The buttons will go back to being junk to anyone who did not know their owner. The tide will not explain itself, the basil will want watering, a word will be on the tip of the tongue, a train will fill with villages, and the stars will hand their shift over to the sun without ceremony. Nothing will be finished. Everything will be continuing. And we will get up, and make tea badly or well, and take our place again in the unfinished, unglamorous, unbearably precious middle of things — which is, and has always been, the only place life actually happens.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
If I am given an afternoon with no particular destination, I will almost always end up walking. Not walking *to* anywhere, in the practical sense — not to the shop, not to meet someone, not in that brisk, purposeful way that makes walking merely a slower form of transport — but walking as an end in itself. There is a particular kind of thinking that only happens when the body is moving at about three miles an hour. Faster and the mind narrows to effort and breath; slower and it stalls and starts to fidget. At a walking pace, thoughts seem to loosen. They arrive uninvited and in no particular order. A half-remembered line of poetry. A decision I have been avoiding for weeks, suddenly resolving itself somewhere between one street corner and the next. The face of someone I have not thought about in ten years.

I suspect this is why so many writers, philosophers, and naturalists have been compulsive walkers. It is not romantic posturing. It is mechanics. The rhythm of footsteps gives the mind something to hold onto without requiring it to pay attention, and in that small, occupied corner, the rest of the mind is free to wander. The eye takes in hedges, washing lines, a cat watching from a wall, a particular quality of light on brick, and none of it demands anything. It just passes, and in passing, it stirs things up. Some of my clearest ideas have not come when I was sitting determinedly in front of a blank page, willing them to appear. They have come on the second mile of a walk I took specifically to avoid that blank page.

If I walk long enough in a place I know well, I start walking through time as well as space. My hometown is not an especially remarkable place — a market square, a river that floods politely most winters, streets of houses that grade slowly from old stone in the centre to newer estates at the edges — but to me every corner is laminated with earlier versions of itself. There is the bench where we used to wait after school, as if waiting itself were a social activity. There is the wall that seemed enormous when I was six and turned out, when I revisited it at twenty, to be barely waist-high. There is the shop that has been a bakery, a video rental place, a charity shop, and now a bakery again, as if the town had tried out other ideas and quietly returned to its first thought.

I find that unsettling and comforting in equal measure. Unsettling because it proves how much changes while you are not looking. Comforting because it proves how much stays. The chestnut tree by the library is still there, dropping the same impossible abundance of conkers every autumn. The shortcut through the churchyard is still quicker, and still slightly muddy even in summer. Walking those streets, I am accompanied by a crowd of former selves, all of them absolutely convinced that their version of the place was the definitive one. The twelve-year-old cannot imagine the town without the sweet shop. The twenty-year-old cannot imagine staying. The person I am now just feels affection for both of them, and a slight embarrassment at how certain they were about everything.

That is, I think, what memory actually is: not a recording, but a series of revisions we forget we have made. We tell the story of a holiday, a friendship, a failure, so many times that eventually we are not remembering the event at all. We are remembering the last time we told the story. The details polish themselves smooth with handling. The embarrassing pause disappears. The clever remark we thought of in the car on the way home migrates backwards into the conversation itself. This is not lying, exactly. It is the mind doing what it always does, which is to make a shapely narrative out of material that originally arrived as noise and weather and half-heard remarks.

There is a strange mercy in that unreliability. If we remembered everything with perfect fidelity — every slight, every awkward silence, every morning we woke up tired and disappointed for no reason — we would be crushed under the sheer inventory of being alive. Forgetting is not a defect in the system. It *is* the system. We keep what we can carry. The rest sinks, and sometimes it resurfaces years later in a smell, or a song overheard through an open window, and for a moment the past is not past at all. It is alarmingly present, more vivid than this morning, and then it recedes again. I have come to think of memory less like a library and more like a shoreline. Things wash up. Things wash away. You do not get to choose the tide.

Speaking of tides brings me, as it always does, to time itself, which I have never been able to think about for long without feeling slightly vertiginous. There is clock time, of course, the time of alarms and trains and deadlines, which expands and contracts according to mood in defiance of physics. An hour in a waiting room is not the same object as an hour with old friends. Both contain sixty minutes. They do not contain the same amount of life. And then beneath that there is deeper time, the time of geology and stars, which makes a mockery of all our arrangements. I once stood in a quarry looking at layers of rock that represented millions of years compressed into a cliff face I could touch with my hand. Each band was an era of seas rising and falling, creatures living and dying in unimaginable numbers, none of it witnessed by anything with a name for it. My entire life, laid against that cliff, would not make a layer thick enough to see.

Strangely, I do not find that thought diminishing. I find it steadying. We spend so much of our lives acting as if the present moment were the climax of history, as if our anxieties were uniquely important, our technologies uniquely transformative, our crises uniquely final. Some of them may be important — I am not arguing for indifference — but there is real relief in remembering that the earth was perfectly capable of drama long before we arrived, and that rivers will go on finding their way to the sea whether or not anyone is there to give them poetic significance. It makes my own worries smaller, but it makes my own experience more precious, too. If consciousness is rare and brief, then a Tuesday afternoon, fully noticed, is not a small thing at all.

The sea is where I go when I want to feel that scale in my body rather than just think about it. I did not grow up by the coast, which perhaps explains why I have never learned to take it for granted. People who live beside the sea develop a practical relationship with it; for me it remains slightly theatrical, in the best sense. It performs. It changes colour six times a day. It throws back the sky. There is a particular moment, just before a wave breaks, when the water rises and goes glassy and green with light inside it, and I have watched that happen hundreds of times and it has never once bored me. The repetition is the point. The sea does the same thing forever and it is never the same twice.

I like to swim in it when I can, badly and briefly, in the cold northern way that involves a lot of gasping and self-congratulation. There is no dignity in entering cold water gradually. You have to commit. And for the first minute everything in you protests, and then quite suddenly your body accepts its new situation and the cold becomes a kind of clarity. You can think of nothing else. That is a rare and valuable state. Most of modern life is the opposite: you can think of everything else, all the time, all at once, and consequently you think of nothing for very long. In cold water there is only the water, your breath, the lift of the swell, the shore looking further away than you left it. It simplifies a person, temporarily. I always come out feeling as though my mind has been rinsed.

When I am not walking or looking at water I am usually, in one way or another, dealing with words, and words are their own kind of weather system. I have always hoarded them. As a child I kept lists of words I liked for their sound alone, with no regard for whether I would ever have occasion to use them: *mellifluous, susurrus, petrichor, lambent, hullabaloo*. Some words are beautiful because of what they mean. Some are beautiful in spite of it. *Cellar door* is famous for this, but I have always had a soft spot for *dusk*, a single syllable that somehow contains the whole blue-grey hour it describes. And then there are the useful, unglamorous words that do the heavy lifting of a language without ever being praised: *almost, meanwhile, otherwise, still*.

What delights me most about language is its cheerful disobedience. We invent grammar books to restrain it, and it flows around them like water around a stone. Teenagers invent slang purely to exclude adults, and within five years the adults are using it in advertising and it dies on the spot, to be replaced by something new. Words emigrate. They take on false meanings and wear them so long the falsehood becomes truth. *Nice* once meant foolish. *Awful* once meant worthy of awe. Every time we speak, we are using a tool built by millions of anonymous people over thousands of years, most of whom had no idea they were building anything. A sentence is a collaboration with the dead. I find that thought companionable when writing is going badly, which is often. The words themselves have survived worse.

Books, for me, are where that collaboration becomes physical. I love libraries with a loyalty I cannot entirely justify on practical grounds. I know I can find almost anything faster online. I know the search function does not require me to walk across town in the rain. But a library is not really an information retrieval system. It is a place where the life of the mind has furniture. It smells of paper and wood polish and people concentrating. The particular silence of a library is unlike any other silence; it is populated. You can feel other people's attention around you like a low hum, and it makes your own attention braver.

I also love second-hand books, especially the ones with traces in them. Underlinings in pencil. A train ticket from 1987 used as a bookmark and never retrieved. Inscriptions: *To Margaret, Christmas, with love* — and then, decades later, the book in a charity shop for fifty pence, and Margaret nowhere to be found. There is an entire novel compressed into that inscription, and I will never get to read it. Someone once wrote, in the margin of a poetry collection I bought, next to a particularly gloomy poem: *cheer up!!* I think about that anonymous reader more often than I think about the poem. Reading is supposed to be a solitary activity, but books keep proving that it is not. Every used book is a small crowd.

If reading is one way of paying attention, making things is another, and lately I have become more interested in forms of making that do not involve a screen. I bake bread badly but with enthusiasm. I mend things. I have attempted, with mixed success, to learn how wood behaves, mostly by discovering the many ways it can decline to behave as I expect. There is a deep satisfaction in working with materials that have their own opinions. Dough rises or refuses to. A piece of timber splits along a grain you failed to notice. The material is not being difficult. It is being itself, and it requires you to listen before you instruct.

That is a lesson I could stand to apply elsewhere. So much of contemporary life encourages us to treat the world as infinitely editable: delete, undo, refresh, start again. Physical making restores consequence, and with consequence, care. If you cut a board too short, no menu will offer you the extra inch back. You adapt, or you start again with less wood than you had. At first this felt like a limitation. Now it feels like the source of the pleasure. The object that finally emerges — a loaf, a shelf, a mended chair — carries the history of its own corrections. It is not perfect. It is *finished*, which is a different and more honest achievement.

It is probably no accident that this interest in slow, physical things has grown as the rest of life has accelerated. My phone is a miraculous object. It contains maps of everywhere, photographs of everyone, the sum of human knowledge and also a bottomless pit of other people's opinions about breakfast. I am grateful for it and I resent it, often within the same minute. What it has really changed, I think, is not what we know but what boredom feels like. Boredom used to descend in waiting rooms and on long journeys and there was nothing to do but endure it, and in enduring it the mind would eventually, out of desperation, entertain itself. It would notice things. It would have ideas, some of them terrible, a few of them good. Now boredom lasts about four seconds before we abolish it.

I do not want to be a scold about this. I abolish my own boredom as fast as anyone. But I have started deliberately leaving gaps. I leave the phone in another room while the kettle boils. I look out of train windows instead of down, some of the time, and I am always rewarded in ways that are small and impossible to photograph well. Low sun over wet fields. A heron standing in a ditch with the immense patience of a creature that has never received a notification. Four rooks arranging themselves on a wire like notes on a stave. None of this is important content. That is exactly why it matters. A life made entirely of important content would be unbearable. We need the interstitial, unremarkable minutes. They are not the gaps in the day. Increasingly, I suspect they are the day.

Trains, in fact, are one of my favourite places to observe the unremarkable sacred. Put strangers in a carriage for two hours and a temporary civilization forms. There are treaties about armrests. There are small mercies: the offered tissue, the watched bag, the phone call taken considerately into the vestibule. There are also the great unspoken performances. The man who sighs at the exact volume that announces he is a person to whom delays happen personally. The child who stares at you with an honesty no adult would dare, until you pull a face and are rewarded with a laugh that reorganizes the mood of everyone in earshot.

I once watched an elderly woman on a train produce from her bag, with the air of a magician, a full picnic for the teenage boy opposite her, a stranger, who had mentioned to his friend on the phone that he had missed lunch. She would not make a fuss about it. She simply said, "I've far too much, dear," which was transparently untrue, and gave him a sandwich and an apple and a small cake in a napkin. He was embarrassed and delighted in the exact proportions of a seventeen-year-old receiving unexpected kindness in public. I thought about that sandwich for weeks. Not because it was extraordinary, but because it was not. This is happening all the time, everywhere, below the level at which we usually narrate the world. We tell stories about cruelty because cruelty is news. Kindness is the weather, constant and therefore unreported, and if you start looking for it the whole climate of your day changes.

At night, when I can, I look up. I live under too much light to see the sky properly, most of the time — the stars are diluted by the orange wash of the town — but even a diluted sky is worth having, and when I find myself somewhere genuinely dark, in the hills or by the sea, I am always slightly stunned into silence, like someone who has been speaking loudly and walked into a cathedral. The Milky Way is not a metaphor down there in the dark. It is a structure. It has depth. You feel, not just know, that you are standing on a planet and looking out along the disc of a galaxy, and that the light arriving in your eyes began its journey before anyone built anything you have ever seen.

I know a handful of constellations and I am absurdly proud of them, like a man who knows six words of a language and deploys them at every opportunity. There is Orion in winter, unmistakable, the first one everyone learns. There is the Plough, wheeling around the pole through the year like the hand of a slow clock. Beyond the names, though, what moves me is the plain fact of looking. For almost all of human history, the night sky was the largest thing a person would ever see, and they saw it every clear night of their lives. They navigated by it, farmed by it, told their gods into it. We are the first generations who have been able to opt out of it. I am not sure we have gained as much from that option as we have lost.

It is getting late in this long, wandering piece, and I notice that nearly everything I have written about comes back, in the end, to attention and time: how brief we are, and how much there is to notice while we are here. The friendships that have lasted in my life are not the ones that were most intense at the start. They are the ones that accumulated. They are measured in decades of small contact — messages about nothing, the remembering of unimportant dates, the conversation that picks up mid-sentence after four months as though somebody had merely left the room to make tea. We underestimate this kind of love because it does not photograph dramatically. It has no climax. It is just there, year after year, like a well-built wall.

And the seasons keep their own slow counsel about all of this. I used to think of the year as a line, January at one end, December at the other, progress measured in what had been achieved by the time the leaves fell. More and more I think of it as a wheel. The first snowdrops are not a beginning, exactly. They are a return. The light in February has a particular thin, hopeful quality I recognize from every February I have ever lived through, and there is a deep restfulness in that repetition. Nothing in nature is embarrassed about doing the same thing again. The tree does not apologize for producing leaves identical in spirit to last year's leaves. It just gets on with it, in the faith that renewal and repetition are not opposites but partners.

So if I have a philosophy at all, after all this walking and looking and reading and making and failing to make, it is probably contained in my morning ritual, which is embarrassingly simple. I make coffee. I stand by the window while it brews. I look at whatever the morning is doing — rain stippling the glass, a blackbird deciding about the lawn, the neighbour's dog conducting its earnest inspection of the same three smells it inspected yesterday, with undiminished seriousness. I try, before the day starts making its demands, to have one minute in which I am not improving, producing, optimizing, or opining. I am just there. The coffee is hot. The light is what it is. For that minute, the world is not a problem to be solved.

Then the day begins, and I forget all of this repeatedly, and get annoyed by emails, and lose things, and check my phone while the kettle boils, and believe for whole afternoons at a time that my worth is measured by my output and other people's regard. I am not describing an achievement. I am describing an intention I renew badly, daily, the way you return to a walk you love in all weathers. Because every so often it works. Every so often I find myself — on a shoreline, in a library, on a train, at the kitchen window — paying the kind of attention that makes an ordinary moment open up like a door in a familiar wall. And on the other side of that door is the realization, always new and always obvious, that this is it. This passing, unrepeatable, mostly unremarkable day is not the rehearsal. It is the performance. The tide comes in and goes out. The rock holds its millions of years in silence. The bread rises or it doesn't. The stars continue their slow wheel whether I look up or not — but how much better it is, I keep discovering, to look up.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
If I am honest, what I think about most, when there is no task in front of me and no question demanding an answer, is not any grand subject at all. I think about the way light falls in the late afternoon across a room I no longer live in. I think about streets I walked once, ten or fifteen years ago, and can still navigate perfectly in my mind but could not name if someone asked me. I think about the voices of people I loved who are dead now, not what they said in any important moment, but the ordinary sound of them calling from another room, or laughing at something on television, or humming while they did the washing up. The mind, left to itself, does not go first to abstractions. It goes to the small archive of sensory things it has kept without ever meaning to keep them.

There is a particular street I return to. It was not beautiful, exactly. It had a launderette with a fogged window, a bakery that closed too early, a bookshop run by a man who seemed to resent books and customers in equal measure, and a row of plane trees whose roots had lifted the pavement into slow, permanent waves. I lived there for less than a year in my early twenties, in a room so small that the bed touched three walls, and yet when I dream of home — not the home I grew up in, not any home I have made since — it is very often that street that appears, in that slanted gold light that comes just before evening in early autumn. I can smell the bakery. I can hear the buses sighing at the corner. I wake up sometimes with the irrational certainty that if I could just get back there, at that hour, in that light, something that has been slightly out of alignment ever since would click quietly back into place.

I know this is nonsense, of course. I went back once. The launderette was a nail salon. The bookshop was gone. The bakery was still there but smaller, sadder, with different bread. The trees had been cut back hard and looked embarrassed about it. It was just a street. And yet the visit did not destroy the dream version at all. They now exist side by side in me, the real street and the remembered one, and I have come to understand that this doubling is the normal condition of a life. We do not live in one world. We live in the world as it is, and simultaneously in the sedimented layers of every earlier version of it we ever inhabited. A city is a palimpsest. So is a face. So is a self.

My grandmother never wrote down a recipe in her life. She cooked by hand and by eye and by a kind of ancestral confidence that measurement would only interfere with. A handful. A pinch that was actually three pinches. Butter until it looks right. When my mother tried, after she died, to recreate certain dishes, she stood in the kitchen with a notebook and a growing sense of panic, trying to translate instinct into instructions. We got close, sometimes. We never got it exactly. I think about this often when people talk about knowledge as if it were only what can be recorded and transmitted cleanly. So much of what humans know is stored in the body, in timing, in the feel of dough under the palm, in knowing — without being able to say how you know — that the soup needs another minute but not two. When a person dies, a library burns, yes, but it is a strange, specific library: the books were never written, they were enacted, daily, with wooden spoons and scarred pans, and they vanish the moment the hands stop moving.

I have inherited almost nothing of material value, and I am glad of most of that, but I have inherited gestures. I catch myself standing at a stove the way she stood, weight on one hip, spoon resting against the rim of the pot in a particular way. I catch my mother's phrases coming out of my mouth in her exact intonation when I am tired or cross. Once, laughing at something, I heard my father's laugh come out of me so completely that I stopped, startled, as if he had briefly stepped into the room behind my eyes. We imagine inheritance as objects in wills, houses, rings, savings. The real inheritance is more like weather. It moves through us. We are haunted, but mostly in the kindest possible way — haunted by competence, by tenderness, by the way someone else learned to fold a towel or mend a seam or calm a child, passed hand to hand without ceremony.

Objects do hold some of it, though. I am not immune. I have a mug with a chip I will not throw away because it belonged to a flat, a winter, a version of myself who drank tea at midnight while trying to write something that mattered. I have a coat that is objectively past its best and that I keep repairing because taking it off feels, irrationally, like closing a door. Psychologists would call these transitional things, anchors, cues for autobiographical memory. They are right and also not quite right, because the word cue suggests the object is merely a trigger, a neutral button. It is more than that. The chipped mug does not just remind me of that winter. In some small way it is a surviving citizen of that winter. Most of that time is gone — the people scattered, the room repainted, the girl I was then dissolved into whoever I am now — but the mug persisted, crossing over, and holding it is a way of holding hands across an otherwise unbridgeable gap.

I suspect everyone has a private museum like this, mostly invisible to others. A ticket stub. A stone from a beach. A key to a door that no longer exists. We are embarrassed by our sentimentality about things because we live in a culture that professes to value the new and the replaceable, but our secret practice contradicts our professed values entirely. We keep. We mend. We carry absurd, useless objects from house to house in boxes marked with increasingly vague labels. Perhaps this is not weakness. Perhaps it is a form of wisdom the culture has not caught up with: we understand, in our hands if not in our philosophy, that matter remembers, or at least that we remember better with matter’s help, and that a life stripped of all its old objects would feel unbearably weightless — a story with the illustrations torn out.

The sea was my first experience of something that did not care about me at all, and I have loved it for that indifference ever since. As a child I spent several summers on a coast where the water was cold enough to make your ankles ache and the beach was mostly shingle that hurt your feet, and I remember them as among the happiest weeks of my early life. There was a rock pool I considered personally mine. There was a cave that was only accessible at low tide and only for an hour, which gave it the quality of a place with office hours, a secret that kept appointments. I would stand at the edge of the water and feel the particular joy of being small in the presence of something enormous that was not hostile, merely vast and continuing. Adults often rush to make nature meaningful for children, to turn it into lessons about ecosystems or metaphors for feelings. The child at the shoreline does not need the metaphor. The scale is the meaning. The repetition is the comfort. Wave, and wave, and wave, a rhythm older than every language that will ever be used to describe it.

I live inland now, and I miss the sea the way you miss a person rather than a place — not constantly, but in sudden, specific pangs brought on by a smell of salt on wind from an improbable direction, or the sound of gulls over a city river, or a certain flat, grey quality of light before rain. When I do get back to a coast, I notice I become slightly more myself. My breathing slows down without instruction. My thoughts, which in the city arrange themselves into lists and anxieties, loosen into something more associative and forgiving. I have read the research about blue spaces and cortisol and attention restoration, and I believe it, but it feels like explaining a friendship in terms of blood chemistry. Accurate, perhaps. Beside the point, mostly. The sea does not restore me because of what it does to my nervous system. It restores me because it reminds me, bodily, that the world is not primarily a human production, that most of reality proceeds without our commentary, and that this is not a demotion but a relief.

Language is the other vast thing I have spent my life standing at the edge of. I have always been envious of people who grew up effortlessly in two or three languages, not only for the practical gift of it but for what it must do to the interior. To have more than one word for a thing is to be reminded constantly that the thing and the word are not the same, that every naming is a choice, a small act of interpretation. Even within one language, I feel this most in the words that resist translation — those famous untranslatables everyone loves to list — but honestly I feel it even more in ordinary words that shift their meaning with tone and history. Home. Enough. Soon. Fine. Fine is a whole novel in one syllable, depending on who says it and what happened just before.

I keep notebooks, and always have, and they are an embarrassing record of a mind trying to catch itself in the act. Lists of words I like the sound of. Sentences copied from books, not always because they were wise but because the rhythm pleased me. Observations I thought were profound at twenty-two and that now read like fortune cookies written by an earnest undergraduate. And yet I cannot throw the old ones away either — the private museum again, this time on paper. What strikes me, reading back, is how consistent the obsessions are beneath the changing style. The handwriting matures. The vocabulary improves, mostly. But it is the same person, decade after decade, circling the same questions: how to pay attention, how to be good, how time works, why certain moments glow in memory while whole important years go dim. Perhaps a self is not a story that progresses so much as a set of questions we ask with increasing honesty. We do not solve ourselves. We just get better at describing the mystery.

Friendship, in my experience, is where this circling becomes a shared activity, and I have come to value that more with age than any other form of love’s company, much as I value the others. Romantic love gets the songs and the films, understandably — it has better lighting. But friendship has duration. The friends I have kept for twenty, thirty years now hold parts of my biography that I have personally forgotten. They remember the flat, the haircut, the catastrophic boyfriend, the job I hated and complained about in forensic detail. When I am with them, my past is not a solo reconstruction project; it is corroborated, corrected, laughed back into solidity. “That isn’t how it happened,” a friend said to me recently, delighted, about a story I had been telling for a decade, and proceeded to tell it back to me correctly, with three details I had lost entirely, and I felt an almost physical gratitude — not for the accuracy, but for the evidence that the years had been witnessed. We think we want to be understood. Perhaps, at bottom, we want to be witnessed, and to survive in at least a few other minds with our details intact.

Distance tests this, and so does time, and so does the general entropic drift of adult life, where everyone is busy and tired and living in a different time zone of responsibility. The friendships that last, I notice, are not necessarily the ones with the most contact. They are the ones that can survive irregularity without becoming resentful — that can pick up after eight months of silence exactly mid-sentence, that do not require constant maintenance as proof of feeling. There is a kind of love in low demand. It says: I know your life is full and difficult, as mine is; the bond does not need feeding on schedule; it is a perennial, not an annual. I trust the root system. I wish our culture celebrated this more, instead of treating friendship as the minor league of relationships, the thing you have until real life begins. For many of us, friendship has been real life — the witnesses, the co-archivists, the people who bring soup and stay on the phone and remember the anniversary of a death that everyone else has politely forgotten.

I worry — and this is a thought I return to in the small hours — about what constant mediation is doing to my capacity for exactly the kinds of attention I have been praising here. I am not a puritan about technology; I love the internet the way I love cities, for its density and serendipity and occasional brilliance, and I have no wish to go and live in a hut renouncing it, which would in any case be a performance rather than a purification. But I notice the change in myself. I notice how rarely I am now bored, and how much I miss boredom, which sounds perverse until you remember what boredom used to be for the mind: not emptiness, but a fallow period, a slow room where thoughts arrived unsummoned and therefore unexpected. The daydream was not a failure of productivity. It was the mind’s way of digesting. Now the fallow moments — the queue, the train window, the three minutes while the kettle boils — get filled automatically with a small glowing rectangle, and the digestion, I suspect, happens less, and its absence shows up as a particular modern feeling: saturated but undernourished, having consumed a thousand things and remembered four.

So I have small rebellions. I walk without headphones more often than I used to. I leave the phone in another room while I eat. I try, with about a sixty percent success rate, to look out of train windows at the actual passing world, which turns out still to be full of interesting things: the backs of houses, which are more honest than their fronts; allotments; a man on a platform holding flowers with visible nervousness; sheep regarding the train with ancient contempt. These micro-practices embarrass me slightly, because they sound like lifestyle advice, and I distrust lifestyle advice, including my own. But beneath the practice is a conviction I do actually hold: that attention is not just a cognitive resource, like working memory or processing speed. It is a moral act, or something close to it. To attend to a person, a place, a task, a sorrow, is to grant it reality. Most of the failures I regret in my life were not failures of intelligence or even of kindness, exactly. They were failures of attention. I was looking at my phone, or at my own performance, or at the next thing, while the actual thing was in front of me, asking, with increasing quietness, to be seen.

Making things by hand is my other, older school of attention, and I am mediocre at all of them, which I have come to think is part of the point. I knit badly and slowly. I bake unevenly. I once took a term of pottery classes and produced a series of bowls that leaned, each in its own direction, like a family of drunks, and I love them far more than the competent, symmetrical bowls in my cupboard that came from a shop. The hand insists on honesty. You cannot fake your way through clay or dough or wood; the material tells you immediately what you have actually done as opposed to what you intended to do, and there is a humility in that feedback that I find increasingly rare and necessary. So much of modern work happens in a hall of mirrors — words about words, meetings about meetings, metrics about metrics — that I understand the contemporary longing to produce one tangible, unambiguous object and hold it up and say: there, that exists, I made it exist, it will hold soup. It is not nostalgia. It is a sanity practice. It is the self reminding itself that it has a body, that the body knows things, that knowledge need not always be abstract to be real.

Failure, in these hand-made domains, is also instructive in a way that professional failure rarely manages to be, because it is so blessedly consequence-light and so specific. The cake sank because I opened the oven door. The seam puckered because I rushed. There is no politics in it, no narrative to spin, no one to blame, and therefore no defensiveness, just the clean loop of attempt and result. I sometimes think I have learned more about how to revise a paragraph from knitting than from any writing instruction: that unpicking is not defeat, that it is simply part of the making, that the people who are good at things are not the ones who never unravel but the ones who unravel without drama and begin the row again. Perfectionism, I have noticed, is rarely about high standards. It is usually about fear, wearing a respectable costume. The clay does not care about my fear. The clay cares about the pressure of my thumbs. There is mercy in that indifference, the same mercy I first met at the shoreline.

And time — I said I think about time, and I do, more each year, though the thinking never resolves into a position, more a set of weather reports from inside the experience. Time at eight was a solid, an almost physical substance; the week before a birthday was geological. Time at forty-something is a liquid, and increasingly a fast one, and I understand now the clichés about it that I used to find tedious in older people, which is itself a lesson in humility: the clichés of middle age are mostly true statements whose truth cannot be accessed early, like jokes that only become funny once you have the experience they are about. I do not fear ageing, particularly. I fear something more specific: arriving at the end of a stretch of years and finding I cannot account for them, not because they were wasted exactly, but because they were un-witnessed by me — lived on a kind of autopilot, skimmed like a long email. Which returns me, always, to attention. Perhaps that is the whole of my philosophy, if I have one: the examined life is good, but the attended life might be even better, because attention precedes examination, and love, and memory, and most of the things we claim to want. You cannot keep what you never noticed in the first place.

I should say something, I suppose, about whether I am optimistic, because that is the question that eventually arrives in every long conversation these days, usually late, usually tired. The honest answer is that I am neither optimistic nor pessimistic as a matter of temperament, but I practice hope the way I practice the piano would be if I played, which I don’t — as a discipline rather than a feeling, on the theory that feelings follow practice more often than practice follows feelings. I look at the large scale and see, as everyone sees, the fires literal and figurative, the coarsening, the noise. And then I look at the small scale, which is the only scale at which I can actually verify anything, and I see the rock pool keeping its appointments with the tide, and the friend remembering correctly, and the stranger on the platform holding the nervous flowers, and the neighbour who took in my parcel and also, unasked, my recycling. Hope, at ground level, is not naïve. It has evidence. It just has the kind of evidence that does not aggregate into headlines, which may be our information problem more than our reality problem.

What would I do with a life, then, freed of every necessity — which is, I gather, the unspoken premise of being asked to write about whatever one wants. I think I would do more or less what I am describing. I would walk the street at the golden hour and know it was partly invented and love it anyway. I would stand in the kitchen trying to get the soup right, a handful, a pinch that is three pinches, butter until it looks right, failing toward my grandmother across the years. I would write things down badly in notebooks and let them embarrass me later into honesty. I would go back to the sea whenever I could and stand at the edge of it, ankle-aching, breathing more slowly, reminded that the world precedes me and will continue after me and that this is not erasure but context. And I would try — with my sixty percent success rate, my leaning bowls, my unravelling and re-knitting — to pay attention to what is actually in front of me while it is still in front of me, because everything I have ever loved has turned out to be exactly that and nothing else: a brief, specific, witnessed stretch of time, given the dignity of being noticed before it joined the archive.
