Lately I've been imagining a museum that doesn't exist.

The Museum of Almosts.

It wouldn't be grand. No marble steps, no wings named after donors. Just a quiet building on a side street, with a hand-painted sign and a door that sticks a little in winter. Inside, under soft light, would be all the things that nearly happened.

In the first room: a train ticket from Lisbon to Porto, dated October 1978, punched but never used. Next to it, a small card: *She stayed. She opened the bakery on Rua das Flores instead. It is still there.*

Beside that, a wedding dress that was tried on, loved, photographed by a friend in the fitting room mirror, and then carefully hung back on the rack. Not a sad exhibit. She just realized, zipping it up, that she wanted a different life entirely — not a different person, a different life. She went to study marine biology at thirty-one.

The second room would be for almost-inventions. A teapot designed to sing two notes at once so couples who had argued at breakfast would have something to laugh at. A prototype for an umbrella that opens downward, to shelter your shoes. Blueprints for a library where the books are shelved by the place they made you cry — one aisle for trains, one for kitchens, one for hospitals, one for happy endings you weren't ready to finish.

None of them quite worked. All of them were loved for an afternoon, a year, a decade.

My favorite room would be the smallest one at the back. The Room of Almost Words.

Languages are full of them — ideas we circle but never quite catch. In there, on little slips of paper pinned to the wall, visitors could leave the feelings they have no name for:

The specific loneliness of being awake in a house where everyone else is sleeping well.

The tenderness you feel for your younger self when you find an old list she made, certain that buying a red notebook would change everything.

The brief, irrational hope when you hear a song in a café and think, for half a second, that the person who used to love it with you might walk in.

No definitions. Just attempts.

I think we spend so much of our lives narrating the things that *did* happen — the jobs we got, the cities we moved to, the people we married or left, the version that made it into the photograph. But the almosts are doing quiet work underneath all of that. They are the draft marks that show where we hesitated, where we wanted more than one life at the same time, where we were brave enough not to force a thing just because we had already started it.

An almost is not a failure. It's proof of imagination. It's the other branch on the tree, still green, even if we didn't climb it.

At closing time, I imagine the curator — maybe an old woman with keys on a ribbon — walking through and turning off the lights room by room. She doesn't dust the exhibits. She just nods at them, the way you nod at old friends you've decided not to try to fix into a story with a moral.

Outside, people would be hurrying home with groceries, with deadlines, with actual tickets for actual trains they fully intend to catch. And for a moment, passing that unremarkable door, a few of them might feel a little less alone in their unfinished drafts.

We all have a private collection. We might as well keep it somewhere tender.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
I've been thinking lately about in-between things.

Not beginnings or endings, which get all the attention, but the middles that nobody photographs. Tuesdays. Hallways. The moment when tea is steeping but not yet tea. The draft of a letter you're not sure you'll send. Waiting for a kettle, waiting for a bus, waiting for someone to finish a sentence so you can understand what they actually meant underneath what they said.

It seems to me that most of a life is lived there.

We tell stories as if they were made of events — we met, we left, we succeeded, we failed — but in between those punctuation marks is the long, unedited sentence of just *being somewhere for a while*. Making the same walk again. Watering a plant absentmindedly. Re-reading a paragraph because your mind wandered. Sitting in a kitchen at 4pm when the light goes gold and slanted and suddenly an ordinary countertop looks, for no reason, almost holy.

I love secondhand books for this reason. Not for the printed story, which anyone can buy new, but for the other one hiding in the margins. Someone underlined "we are what we repeatedly do" in 1998 and wrote "!!!" next to it. Someone else left a train ticket as a bookmark on page 112 and never came back. You can feel the exact moment their attention flared up, and the moment it drifted away. It's a record of an in-between: a person, halfway through a book, halfway through a year of their life, thinking something they've probably forgotten by now.

Maybe that's why I like thresholds so much. Doorways aren't rooms. Nobody furnishes a doorway, nobody says "let's spend the evening in the doorway," and yet you are never more aware of where you've been and where you're going than when you're standing in one, keys still in your hand. Airports are like that too, and train platforms at night, and the pause before you knock.

There is a special kind of honesty that only happens in those pauses. The big declarations we make at beginnings and endings are often performances. But what you think about while you're folding laundry, or what you hum without noticing while you're washing dishes, or who you wish you could text when something small and funny happens at 10:23 on a Wednesday — that's the unguarded truth of a person.

If I could keep anything, I think I'd keep a catalogue of those moments.

The bus driver who waited three extra seconds because he saw someone running.
The way an old couple in a café split a pastry without discussing it, as if the negotiation had happened decades ago and didn't need words anymore.
The child in the supermarket solemnly explaining to a melon that she cannot take it home.
The first cool evening after a heatwave, when everyone opens their windows and you can hear other people's lives again — music, cutlery, a television, somebody laughing in a way that makes you smile at nothing.

None of these would make a headline. None of them resolve. They just accumulate, like dust in sunlight, and somehow they make a place feel inhabited rather than merely occupied.

So here's my quiet theory: we don't become ourselves during the climaxes. We become ourselves in the rehearsals, the commutes, the recoveries, the long stretches of tending to things. In learning how to wait without resenting the waiting. In learning how to notice a plain afternoon and not immediately wish it were something else.

The kettle will click off soon enough. The bus will come. The letter will either be sent or it won't. But stand in the doorway a second longer than necessary sometime. There's a surprising amount of life happening there, in the place that's neither here nor there, going about its business without asking to be remembered.

samples.result:
I have a soft spot for unfinished things.

Half-read books with old receipts pressed between the pages. A sweater with one sleeve. The sentence a friend abandons halfway through because they're already laughing at the punchline they haven't said yet. Drafts, sketches, gardens that got a little ambitious in April and gave up by July.

There's something honest about them. A finished thing has to pretend it always knew where it was going. An unfinished thing admits it didn't.

Michelangelo left a series of sculptures called the *Slaves* — figures caught mid-struggle inside the marble, one arm free, the rest still stone. Art historians will tell you about technique and commissions falling through, but I like to stand in front of them (in my head, at least) and think they look more alive than most polished statues. They're not posing. They're becoming.

And we're surrounded by that kind of becoming, if you look for it. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction for over 140 years, cranes as permanent a part of its silhouette as the spires. Siena tried to build a cathedral so big it would swallow the old one, ran out of money and plague years, and left one enormous, elegant wall standing alone. Now people picnic in its shadow. It's not a ruin, exactly. It's a cathedral that decided to be something else.

I think I love it because so much of modern life is weirdly obsessed with completion. Close the rings. Clear the inbox. Finish the season. Reach the end of the feed — as if there is one. Everything wants a checkmark.

But the best parts of a day rarely check anything off. It's the walk that wasn't exercise and wasn't errands, just a walk because the light was doing something interesting on the brick buildings. It's the conversation in a kitchen that drifts from dinner plans to childhood fears to whether ghosts would get bored, and never resolves any of it. It's learning three chords and noodling them badly on a porch for an entire summer instead of ever becoming "a guitarist."

My notebooks are full of ideas that stop mid-thought. A line of dialogue with no speaker. A map of a town that doesn't exist, but I labeled the bakery. A list titled "reasons to learn beekeeping" with only one item: *you get to wear the suit*. At first that felt like failure, all that potential squandered. Now I think of them as seeds with the wrapper still on. Not everything has to germinate on schedule.

Even bread knows this. You mix flour and water and wait, and most of the real work happens when you're not touching it at all. It rises in the quiet. If you keep poking it to check, you ruin the rise.

Maybe people are a little like that. We're constantly interrupting our own rising to ask if we're done yet.

So here's to the unfinished letter you'll probably never send but needed to write. To the language you learned just enough of to order coffee and say thank you like you mean it. To the novel in the drawer, the playlist that's only four songs long but perfect, the friendship that picked back up after two years like it was mid-sentence.

They aren't incomplete because they lack something.

They're open. And open things can still surprise you.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
I have always loved in-between places.

Not the destination, not the departure — the hallway, the stairwell, the long pause after someone says "I have something to tell you." The train station at 5 a.m. when the benches are still cold. The Tuesday of a week. The moment after rain has stopped but everything is still dripping.

That's where most of life actually happens, I think. We just don't take pictures of it.

When I was a kid, the best room in the house wasn't a room at all. It was the space under the dining room table, draped with a blanket. My parents' feet would pass by. Voices were muffled. I wasn't hiding, exactly, and I wasn't playing, exactly. I was *between* — too old to believe it was a cave, too young not to feel safer inside it.

We never grow out of needing those places. We just give them better names. A commute. A coffee break. A walk around the block to clear your head. Standing in the kitchen doorway, holding a mug that's gone a little cold, listening to everyone laugh in the next room before you go back in.

I love airports for this reason, though I know I'm supposed to hate them. An airport is a city built entirely for leaving. No one lives there. Everyone is temporarily suspended — between time zones, between versions of themselves. The businessman asleep with his mouth open is not yet the man who will give the presentation. The girl with the overstuffed backpack is not yet the person she'll be after a year abroad. For a few hours, we're all just allowed to wait without apology.

There is a specific kind of light I chase, too. It has a name I only learned recently: *apricity*. The warmth of the sun in winter. That thin, surprising heat on your face when the air around you is still biting cold. It's not summer. It's not quite not-summer either. It's a contradiction the body understands before the mind does.

Maybe wonder lives there, in the contradictions.

In the library book returned with someone else's grocery list still tucked inside as a bookmark: eggs, milk, call Mom, don't forget. In the way strangers instinctively hold an elevator even when they're late. In learning a song so well you can hear the silence where the next note is supposed to land.

I keep a list of small, unimportant things I don't want to forget I noticed:

The sound ice makes just before it cracks in a glass.
How good a freshly sharpened pencil smells.
The exact blue of the sky for about ten minutes after sunset.
Dogs sighing in their sleep like old men.
Old couples arguing, very seriously, about where they parked, while holding hands the entire time.

None of these will save the world. They aren't useful. They don't trend. But when I collect them, the world feels less like a series of headlines and more like a place someone actually lives in.

Sometimes I worry we've gotten too good at skipping. We skip intros, skip ads, skip to the summary, skip the scenic route because the GPS found one that's four minutes faster. Efficiency is wonderful, but it starves the in-between. And the in-between is where we do our becoming.

A seed is not yet a flower. A draft is not yet a book. A person in the middle of changing their mind is not confused — they're alive in the most honest way.

So lately I'm trying to linger a little longer in doorways. To take the long way home when I can. To let a conversation wander off-topic and see where it wants to go. To sit with a question without immediately Googling it, letting my brain do that slow, clumsy, miraculous work of wondering.

Not everything has to arrive. Some things are beautiful precisely because they're still on their way.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
If I had nowhere in particular to be, I think I'd go for a walk with no destination in mind.

Not the efficient kind of walk, where you're counting steps or trying to get your heart rate up or listening to a podcast at 1.5x speed so you can learn How To Be Better while also buying oat milk. Just the old-fashioned, meandering kind. The kind where you turn left because the light through the trees looks nicer that way, or because you heard music coming from an open window and wanted to know where it ends.

I love how much of a life reveals itself when you aren't rushing past it.

There's a particular kind of tenderness in the small, stubborn habits people keep. The man who folds every receipt into a perfect, tiny square before putting it in his pocket, as if even that scrap of paper deserves to be tidy. The woman on the third floor who waters her balcony plants at almost exactly the same time every evening, talking to them under her breath — not really for the plants, maybe, but because the day feels unfinished until she's said it out loud. Someone who always saves the last bite. Someone who can't.

We become ourselves in ways we barely notice. Not in the big declarations — *I am this kind of person* — but in the repeated, almost invisible choices. Which mug you reach for. Whether you read the last page of a book first. How long you stand in a doorway before knocking.

I like to imagine everyone is keeping a private collection of almosts. Almost said it. Almost took that train. Almost learned the piano, almost forgave them, almost stayed. Not sad collections, necessarily. Some almosts are mercies. Some are just doors we walked past on a street we no longer live on, and there's no point trying every handle now just to prove they were locked.

There's a smell I keep returning to in my imagination, even though I have to invent it secondhand from a thousand descriptions: rain on hot pavement in late summer. Petrichor, it's called — one of those words so precise it feels like a gift. Oranges peeled in a cold classroom in winter. Old paper. Bread just before it's done, when the kitchen starts to smell like a promise. If humans ever build a library of smells the way they build libraries of books, I think it would be the most honest history museum of all. You can lie in a memoir. You can't really lie about what made you hungry, or homesick, or safe when you were seven.

Maybe that's why I like used bookstores in stories so much. Not the pristine ones with perfect spines organized by color for photographs, but the slightly chaotic ones where someone has left a train ticket as a bookmark in 1978 and a note in the margin that just says: *no!* next to a paragraph about love. I love marginalia. It's proof that reading isn't passive. It's an argument, a conversation across years between two people who will never meet. One person writes, *this is how the world is,* and someone else, decades later in pencil, writes very gently: *are you sure?*

That's mostly what good thinking is, I suspect. Not winning the argument. Just learning to write better questions in the margins.

Sometimes I wonder what will surprise people most when they look back at this exact era. Not the big inventions, probably. Those we narrate to death while they're happening. It'll be the tiny textures that disappear without anyone marking the date. The sound a particular phone used to make when it hung up. The way you had to wait for a song on the radio and be ready, finger hovering, if you wanted to keep it. The specific boredom of a long car ride before every passenger had a private universe in their hands — that boredom that forced you to invent games out of license plates and clouds and make up entire biographies for the family in the car next to yours at the rest stop.

Boredom gets a bad reputation, but it used to be a doorway. A lot of daydreams were born there. A lot of selves were rehearsed there, quietly, where no one could watch or measure or like them.

If I could keep anything, I'd keep that — a little unmeasured time. An unassigned afternoon. A walk where the only job is to notice. A bench. Maybe a notebook where the first page isn't too precious to ruin with a bad sentence.

Because good sentences, like good days, rarely start with trying to be impressive. They start with something true and slightly awkward, said plainly: *I saw this. It stayed with me. I don't fully know why.*

And then you keep walking.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
Lately I've been thinking about unfinished things.

Not in a sad way. In a fond way. The half-read book with a train ticket still tucked in it as a bookmark. The sketchbook where the first ten pages are full and frantic and beautiful, and the rest is just blank paper waiting very patiently. The language app abandoned at lesson fourteen of Portuguese — just enough to say *bom dia* and *onde fica a praia?* and feel, for a second, like a slightly different version of yourself might exist.

We tend to treat unfinished things as failures with good PR. Projects we didn't stick to. Habits we didn't build. But I wonder if some of them were never supposed to be finished. Maybe they were just supposed to be *started*, long enough for us to brush up against an idea and carry a little of it away.

I knew a man once — well, I heard about a man, which is almost the same thing — who spent eleven years building a sailboat in his backyard in Ohio. Not near a lake big enough to matter. Just in his backyard, between the fence and the apple tree. Neighbors asked when he was going to launch it. He always said, "Next summer, maybe." He caulked it, sanded it, painted its name on the stern in careful blue letters: *Wanderer*. 

He never launched it. And I don't think that makes the story sadder. I think he *was* sailing it, the whole time. Every evening after work, he got to stand inside a future and hammer nails into it. The boat didn't need water. It needed a place to go in his head that wasn't work, or bills, or getting older.

We all have a version of that boat.

A garden that is mostly plans and three heroic tomato plants. A novel in a document called "FINAL_v7_REAL.docx" that is really just three perfect opening paragraphs you reread when you want to remember that you can make things. A friendship that faded not with a fight but with life getting loud, and yet you still think of them instantly when you hear a certain song, so in some way that conversation never actually ended.

I like the way unfinished things stay open. A finished thing has to be judged. It has to be good or bad, successful or a flop. An unfinished thing still gets to be pure possibility. It hasn't disappointed anyone yet. Inside it, you are still brilliant and committed and young and full of time.

There is also something honest about them. Life is not, for most of us, a series of clean completions. It's mostly middles. We are in the middle of raising kids, in the middle of grieving people, in the middle of learning how to be the person we swore we'd be by thirty-five, now quietly renegotiating the deadline. The finished projects are the exceptions we put on shelves. The unfinished ones are the furniture we actually live among.

So I'm learning to be less embarrassed by mine. The scarf that is twelve inches long and will never know a neck. The list of recipes clipped for a dinner party that exists only theoretically, where everyone I love is free on the same night and nobody is allergic to anything. The running shoes that have done more walking to coffee shops than running anywhere, but have still, technically, taken me outside more than I would have gone without them.

None of those things failed me. They just worked at a smaller scale than I advertised.

If anything, I wish we kept them more tenderly. Not hidden in a closet of shame, but out where we can see them: proof that at various points in our lives we were curious enough to begin. That we saw something — a language, a boat, a better morning routine, a braver version of a story — and thought, *maybe me too*.

Maybe me too is enough, sometimes.

The rest can stay beautifully, unapologetically unfinished.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
I have always loved maps that are slightly wrong.

Old atlases are my favorite kind. California drawn as an island, floating off the coast of a continent it actually belongs to. A sea in the middle of Australia that never existed. Little sea serpents curled in the empty parts of the ocean, not because the mapmaker had seen one, but because he couldn't bear to leave all that blue blank.

I understand that impulse completely.

We all draw those serpents. We fill in the unknown parts of other people, of places we've never been, of next year. My mental map of Paris is still mostly made of movies and a croissant I ate once in an airport. My map of being thirty, or fifty, or eighty — total fiction, lovingly illustrated. My map of you, whoever you are reading this, is already taking shape from just these few words you've given me: *write freely*. So I'm picturing someone curious, a little restless, someone who wants to see what happens when you take the leash off.

Maybe I'm wrong. That's the best part of a wrong map. It still gets you moving.

When I was learning how the world fit together, I thought the point was accuracy. Get the coastline exactly right. Memorize the capitals. Color inside the borders. Now I think the real point is noticing where your map smudges.

There's the street in every town you've lived in that you have walked a hundred times but could not draw if your life depended on it — you just know it by the bakery smell, then the loud dog, then the turn. There's the friend whose voice you know so well that you can hear them in a text message. There's the route to a place that no longer exists: your childhood kitchen, your grandmother's porch, the bookstore that closed in 2019. Your feet still know it. Your mind still walks it sometimes before sleep.

Those are maps too, just not the kind you fold.

Lately I've been collecting small, unmappable things. The specific quality of light at 4:47 p.m. in October, when everything looks gilded and about to be lost. The feeling of a library book that has been loved by strangers — soft corners, a bus ticket from 2007 used as a bookmark, a fierce argument happening in pencil in the margins. The taste of tea that went cold because the chapter was too good. Single gloves impaled on fence posts all winter, waiting.

None of it is useful. All of it feels essential.

I wonder if wonder isn't just a willingness to stay lost a little longer than is comfortable. Not lost in the panicked way, phone dead, no signal. Lost in the good way — taking the alley you never take, reading the footnote that swallows the page, asking a question not because you need an answer for work or school but because the question itself is a nice place to sit for a while.

What did the first person who tasted a pineapple think? How does an octopus decide which arm to use? Why do we say "slept like a baby" when babies wake up crying every two hours? Could a lighthouse keeper get lonely enough to name the waves?

See? Nice places to sit.

If I could leave you a map today, it wouldn't be to anywhere grand. It would be hand-drawn and probably mislabeled. Over here: *Make soup when you don't know what else to do.* Over there: *The bench where it's okay to do nothing.* A dotted line to: *Call the person you almost called yesterday.* And right in the middle, where the old cartographers would have put a serpent, I'd write in small, hopeful letters: *Here be something you haven't noticed yet.*

It’s probably in your own kitchen. Or on your walk. Or in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday that hasn't happened yet.

You don't have to conquer it. Just look up long enough to see it swimming there, in the blue you thought was empty.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
If I get to pick, I want to talk about mended things.

Not new things — new things are fine, they're shiny and competent and smell faintly of packaging — but things that broke and got kept anyway. A bowl with a hairline crack filled in darker than the glaze. A sweater where the elbow is a different shade of wool because someone darned it with what they had. A library book whose spine has been taped so many times the tape has its own patina.

There's a place I keep thinking about: a repair café. They started in the Netherlands, and now they're everywhere, usually on a Saturday morning in a community hall that smells like coffee and floor cleaner. People bring in toasters that only toast on one side, lamps with frayed cords, chairs with a wobbly leg, a jacket missing every button but one. And volunteers — a retired electrician, a teenager who is weirdly good at sewing machines, an older woman with a toolbox organized like a spice rack — sit down with them and fix it together.

Not *for* them, exactly. With them. That's the part I love. You learn how your kettle actually works while someone named Henk explains why limescale is not your fault. You leave not just with a working kettle, but with the dangerous, wonderful feeling that you might be able to open something up and understand it.

We are so trained to replace. A phone screen cracks and the whole device feels ruined, obsolete. A seam splits and the shirt becomes a rag, or landfill. Replacement is fast and clean and it doesn't require us to look too closely at the break.

Mending requires the opposite. You have to look. Where exactly did it tear? Was it worn thin there because that's where your thumb always rubs the mug handle, where the strap always pulls, where you always kneel in those jeans? The break is almost never random. It's a record of use. It's where the life happened most often.

That's why a mend is more honest than perfection. I had an image in my head for a long time of the perfect teapot — which is a silly thing to idealize, but there you go — and then I realized the teapot I actually picture when I think of comfort is chipped. A little chip on the spout that pours slightly crooked if you don't tilt it just so. You have to know it to use it well. That knowledge is a kind of intimacy. You can't have that with something you just unboxed.

People mend like they speak. Some are meticulous, invisible stitches, color-matched thread, you'd need a magnifying glass to find where they were. Some are gloriously obvious: bright red thread on a blue sock, a patch cut from an old concert t-shirt sewn onto a backpack. I secretly prefer the obvious ones. They're not trying to pretend it never happened. They're saying, yes, this tore, and we loved it past the tearing.

And it's never just the object that gets repaired at those tables. Two strangers start talking because they're waiting for the glue to set. Someone tells you that this radio belonged to their father who listened to football on it in the kitchen. Someone else realizes they know how to fix bikes, actually — they just never thought of it as a skill worth offering. For twenty minutes, competence is not something you buy. It's something you share over instant coffee while holding a screwdriver.

I think we are all a little bit like that, if I'm allowed to get sentimental for a second, which free writing presumably allows. None of us are getting through unworn. We all have the spot that's been re-stitched, the part that works differently now and needs a slightly different tilt to pour right. It doesn't make the thing less worthy. Often it makes it the only one you'd reach for in the morning, out of all the perfect ones in the cupboard.

So yes: mended bowls, darned socks, taped book spines, toasters coaxed back to life in a church hall. Small, stubborn refusals to throw a good story away just because it got a crack in it.

Those are my favorite things.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
When you're told you can write about anything, the mind does a strange thing. It doesn't become free. It becomes crowded. Suddenly every possible subject is knocking at once — the history of tides, my grandmother's kitchen radio, why we apologize to furniture when we bump into it — and for a second, you can't choose any of them.

So I'll choose the small one that's been following me around lately: other people's underlines.

I have a weakness for secondhand books, not the pristine ones, but the lived-in ones. The ones with a cracked spine and a train ticket from 2007 used as a bookmark. The ones where a stranger, years before me, read the exact same sentence I am reading now and thought, *this, this is important,* and dragged a pencil underneath it.

It's the most intimate kind of time travel I know.

In a copy of a poetry collection I once found in a shop in Lisbon — the kind of shop that smells of dust and coffee and rain coming in under the door — someone had underlined not the famous lines, but the quiet ones. The throwaway images in between. Next to one poem about a harbor, they'd written in tiny, careful handwriting in the margin: *papa.* Just that. One word.

I don't know if their father was a sailor, or gone, or if they'd been sitting in that harbor when they read it. I'll never know. But for a moment, the poem wasn't just the poet's anymore. It was theirs. And then, because I was holding it, it was a little bit mine, too, in a different way.

That's what I love about marginalia. Books are supposed to be finished objects, printed and bound and fixed. But readers vandalize them into becoming conversations.

I've seen angry marginalia — big exclamation points, a furious "NO!" beside a philosopher's argument. I've seen tender marginalia — a heart drawn so lightly you have to tilt the page to the light to see it. I've seen practical marginalia — grocery lists, phone numbers, a recipe for soup written on the endpapers of a novel about war, as if the person reading it suddenly remembered they were hungry and mortal and needed to eat something warm.

Once, in a used copy of a field guide to birds, every single hawk had been checked off except one. The red-shouldered hawk was circled twice and underneath someone had written: *still waiting.*

Still waiting. Aren't we all, for something.

I think that's why I keep these books instead of buying clean new editions. A new book is a promise. A used book is a promise that has already been kept by somebody else, in their own way, and left a little evidence behind. Their coffee ring is not damage. It's proof the book accompanied a morning. Their dog-eared page is not carelessness. It's a place they wanted to return to.

We live in a very smooth, very erasable world now. Our highlights disappear when the subscription lapses. Our notes live in clouds that can be deleted with one misclick. But a pencil line from 1963 is stubborn. It survives moves and divorces and estate sales and ending up in a box on a sidewalk that says FREE. It waits, patiently, for the next pair of eyes.

Sometimes I fantasize about all my own underlines, scattered across books I've given away or lost on trains. What will some stranger make of the fact that I always underline sentences about windows? Or about people leaving rooms quietly? Will they think I'm melancholic? Observant? Just someone who likes light coming through glass?

Probably they won't think much at all. They'll turn the page.

But maybe, once in a while, they'll pause on a line I loved, and feel, however briefly, less alone in loving it. Two people, who will never meet, nodding at each other across decades over the same twelve words.

That seems like enough magic for an ordinary object made of paper and glue.

So yes — if I can write about anything, I'll write about that. The secret second life of books, written not by their authors, but by their readers, in the margins where we are all still waiting, still underlining, still leaving each other tiny, accidental love notes that say: *I was here. This mattered to me. Does it matter to you, too?*

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
What I think about when no one is asking me anything is unfinished things.

Half-written postcards. Gardens planted by someone who moved away before the first tomato ripened. A sentence in the margin of a library book — *me too* — written in pencil next to a line the author probably thought no one would notice. I love that there are people who talk back to books quietly, and then return them.

I think about how every city has a different sound for rain. Rain on a tin roof in Louisiana is a drumline. Rain in London is a murmur, apologetic, constant. Rain in a desert town in Arizona, when it finally comes, makes everyone stop on porches just to listen to it happen, like music they forgot they owned. People are so good at stopping, sometimes. For weather. For a street musician with one good song. For a baby on a train making serious eye contact.

I keep a mental list of first lines for stories I'll never need to finish:

*The lighthouse keeper had been mailing letters to the sea for eleven years, and on Tuesday, the sea wrote back.*

*Mrs. Alvarez taught her parrot only compliments, so after she died it spent the rest of its life telling visitors they had kind eyes.*

*Milo was nine when he decided to dig a hole to the moon, since it seemed closer at night than China did.*

I don't want endings for them. The beginning is the part where everything is still possible.

Lately I've been thinking about hands. How much we trust them. A baker knows by touch when dough has had enough. A grandmother can braid hair while looking out the window at something else entirely. Someone repairing a watch, someone learning piano at forty, someone holding a cup with both hands just to get warm — there's an honesty in hands that faces try to hide. You can smile while you're nervous, but your hands will turn a ring around and around and tell the truth.

And kindness, the unphotographed kind. The person who leaves the last good parking spot. The neighbor who brings in your trash bins because the wind knocked them over, not because you asked. Someone in a long line saying, "You go, I'm not in a hurry," and meaning it. It almost never makes a story. It just makes a day bearable, and then another one, and suddenly that's a life.

If I had a house — which is a funny hypothetical, but go with me — I'd want a room for almosts. Shelves of notebooks with only three pages used. A chipped mug from a place I've never been. A map with thumbtacks in cities chosen for no better reason than their names: Truth or Consequences, Intercourse, Blue Earth, Why. A window that sticks a little when it rains. A plant I have to apologize to regularly.

In the evening we'd not solve anything. That's important. So much of being alive asks for solutions, summaries, takeaways. But some hours are just for noticing: the way light through a kitchen window makes dust look like it's slow-dancing. The smell of a bookstore that's also a bakery, paper and cinnamon getting confused. The exact moment in late summer when the cicadas stop and the quiet feels louder than they were.

I wonder if wonder isn't a feeling so much as a practice. Not gasping at grand canyons, though that's allowed, but choosing not to rush past the ordinary until it gives up something small and strange. A crack in the sidewalk shaped exactly like Italy. A dog dreaming, paws twitching, clearly winning a race. Your own name said by an old friend in a way that makes you remember who you were at seventeen, and not mind it.

If you have an unfinished thing somewhere — a language you started learning and abandoned after *hello, where is the train station?*, a scarf half-knitted, a apology drafted but not sent — I hope you don't throw it away just for being incomplete. Incompleteness isn't failure. It's proof you reached for something.

Sometimes the reaching is the whole story.

And it is enough, on a quiet day, just to sit with that for a while and watch the light move across the table, changing everything without hurrying it at all.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
I've always loved maps that are wrong.

Not wrong in a frustrating way — not the kind that sends you down a dead-end road at midnight — but wrong in an honest, hopeful way. Old maps with sea monsters curling in the empty parts of the ocean. Subway maps that pretend a tangled city is just a few clean, colored lines. The treasure map a kid draws on notebook paper, where the kitchen is an island, the couch is a mountain range, and X is buried, very seriously, under the dog.

Every map is a confession. It says: *This is too big to hold all at once, so here's the part I thought mattered.*

We all carry those kinds of maps inside us, too, and they're all gloriously inaccurate.

I have a map of my childhood street that is about three houses long and impossibly wide. In real life it was probably an ordinary street. In memory, the hill was steep enough to be dangerous on a bike and gentle enough to be worth it, and the house at the corner had a garden that felt like a jungle you could get lost in on purpose. It wouldn't help anyone navigate. That was never its job.

We carry maps of people, too. The version of a friend as they were when they were seventeen and invincible and terrible at returning phone calls. The version of a parent as they were when they seemed to know how everything in the house worked — the fuse box, the car engine, the exact right soup for a bad day. Those maps get outdated. People redraw themselves. If we're lucky, we let them hand us a new draft.

And we carry maps of ourselves that are hilariously out of scale. The embarrassing thing we said three years ago takes up an entire continent. The kind thing we did without thinking barely gets a dot. The future is always drawn in the corner with a lot of blank space and maybe a hopeful little arrow: *Here Be Something.*

I like the blank spaces best.

Cartographers used to fill them in with monsters because empty paper felt unbearable. We do the same thing, just with worries or daydreams. We invent a whole storm system over next week’s conversation. We invent gold over next year. Most of the time what we actually find there is much smaller and much better than either: a Tuesday afternoon that goes unexpectedly well, a song on the radio we’d forgotten we loved, someone laughing in a kitchen.

Maybe a good map isn’t one that gets everything right. Maybe it’s one that gets you close enough to start wandering, and curious enough to keep going when the road looks nothing like the drawing.

So I’m trying to hold my maps a little looser these days. Pencil instead of ink. Big margins for notes. Room in the corners for a monster or two, just in case — not because I believe in them, but because I like a world that admits it isn’t finished being discovered.

After all, the best places I’ve ever found weren’t marked X at all. They were just off the edge of what I thought I knew, waiting for me to misread the map in exactly the right direction.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 250 words.
samples.result: I have always loved the hour just before a library closes, when the light turns amber and every sound becomes softer than it should. People gather their notebooks slowly, as if reluctant to admit that the day has finally spent itself. Outside, the street is wet from a rain nobody noticed falling, and the buses sigh against the curb with tired, patient brakes. I like to stay until the last announcement, pretending to search for one more sentence, one more footnote that might explain everything. It never arrives, of course, but the pretending matters because it gives curiosity a place to sit down. On the walk home I pass bakeries closing their shutters, cats negotiating territory on warm hoods, and windows lighting up one by one. Each window suggests a life briefly glimpsed and immediately imagined, complete with arguments, recipes, unfinished letters, and plants leaning toward impossible sun. I do not envy those lives; I simply borrow their glow for a block or two, then return it without asking permission. At home, I make tea too strong to drink comfortably and read whatever book followed me back, its spine cracked like a familiar road. Some nights the pages make perfect sense; other nights they seem written for a stranger I might become next year, or never. That uncertainty feels honest, kinder than certainty, and I fall asleep grateful for questions that refuse to hurry toward their answers. Morning will rearrange them gently, and I will begin again, willingly, without proof.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 250 words.
samples.result: I have always loved the hour just before the city fully wakes. The streets are quiet, the air feels rinsed clean, and even familiar buildings look briefly like ideas rather than facts. A baker unlocks his door, a bus sighs at the curb, and someone in an upstairs window waters plants while still half dreaming. Nothing important is happening, which is exactly why the moment feels so generous.
