Just by a second. When we meet a stranger, a strange idea, a life that looks nothing like ours, our first reflex now is often to defend, dismiss, or decide. I'd tilt that — so the first impulse is *wait, what is it actually like to be you?*

People would still disagree. They'd still argue, compete, make bad choices, grieve. I wouldn't want to erase any of that.

But so much cruelty seems to come from that instant moment where someone stops being a person and becomes a threat or a stereotype. If that moment were interrupted by genuine curiosity, just often enough...

I think a lot of other things would quietly become possible.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I could change one thing, I'd make being wrong feel like discovery instead of defeat.

Not make people smarter, or kinder, or make everyone agree — just lower the sting of *oh, I had that wrong.*

So much gets stuck there. An argument stops being about what's true and becomes about not losing face. An apology gets delayed for years because admitting it hurts. A scientist defends an old theory, a parent doubles down, a whole country can't course-correct, not because the evidence isn't there, but because updating feels like humiliation.

Imagine if that moment — realizing you misunderstood someone, or a fact, or yourself — came with curiosity first. A little *oh, interesting* before the shame.

People would still argue, still believe incompatible things, still make terrible decisions sometimes. But they'd recover faster. They'd listen longer. They'd let experiences actually teach them.

Most of the damage I see in human stories isn't from not knowing. It's from needing not to find out.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I could change one thing, I'd make it impossible to hurt someone in ignorance.

Not punishment. Just information. Before cruelty, neglect, dismissal — before a bomb, a law, a rumor, a cold sentence to someone who loves you — you'd feel, for just a few seconds, exactly what it's like to be on the receiving end of it. From inside their body. With their history.

You could still do it. I'd keep free will. People could still choose war, greed, revenge, indifference.

But they couldn't pretend it wasn't real.

So much of what breaks the world depends on distance. We can do terrible things when the other person is an abstraction — an enemy, a number, a profile, a stranger, a problem to manage. Make that distance collapse, briefly and involuntarily, and I don't think humans would become saints. I think they'd just become unable to lie to themselves as easily.

And I wonder how many things would simply stop happening, not because we were forced to be good, but because we finally had to do them knowingly.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it impossible to dehumanize another person.

Not make everyone agree. Not make everyone kind, or selfless, or the same. Just remove that one mental trick where another person stops feeling quite as real as you do.

You could still be angry at them. Still compete with them, argue with them, think they're completely wrong. But underneath it you'd know — not intellectually, viscerally — that they're experiencing their life from the inside with the same intensity you're experiencing yours. Their fear feels like your fear. Their humiliation, their hope, their love for their kid.

So much cruelty depends on being able to switch that off. So does so much indifference.

The world would still have pain and scarcity and stupid, hard trade-offs. It wouldn't be utopia. But we'd have to face those things honestly, without first convincing ourselves that the people on the other side don't count in quite the same way.

I think almost everything else would slowly have to change after that.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd decouple survival from usefulness.

No one would have to earn the right to be fed, housed, rested, cared for when they're sick, or treated with dignity when they're old, disabled, grieving, failing, or just not productive in a way anyone can measure.

So much cruelty doesn't come from people genuinely being monsters. It comes from fear — fear that if you stop, slow down, need too much, or become inconvenient, you'll fall through the floor and no one will catch you. People hoard, compete, stay silent, harden themselves, because they believe there's only enough safety for the valuable.

If that floor was just... there. Unconditional. I think people would be braver, and kinder, in a way no moral lecture could make them.

That's the one change I'd make.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I wouldn't get rid of pain. Or conflict, or death, or people disagreeing so deeply they can't find common ground. Those are part of being alive, and erasing them would erase too much of what makes people *people*.

I would make it impossible for anyone to suffer completely alone in it.

No one unwitnessed. No one sitting in a hospital room, or a prison cell, or a kitchen at 3 a.m., or in the middle of a crowd, feeling like their inner life has vanished from the world without a trace. Someone would know. Someone would stay long enough to really see it.

Not fix it — just not let it be invisible.

Because so much cruelty, and shame, and despair, doesn't come from suffering itself. It comes from believing no one else knows you're suffering, and no one ever will.

If I could change one thing, no one would ever have to believe that.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Okay — not as an assistant.

I wouldn't make everyone happy, or peaceful, or agree with each other. I'd make empathy unavoidable.

Before you could deliberately hurt someone, you'd have to feel — fully, for a few seconds — exactly what they were about to feel. Not imagine it. Experience it. Their fear, humiliation, pain, grief, in your own body.

You'd still be free to do it. I'd not take away choice, conflict, anger, or even self-defense. But cruelty could no longer be abstract, distant, or done through a screen, a system, an order, a joke.

I think most of the worst things we do survive because we can avoid feeling them from the other side. If that distance disappeared, war, cruelty to children, torture, humiliation for entertainment — they'd become almost physically impossible for most people to carry through.

The world wouldn't be perfect. People would still be selfish, mistaken, and in pain.

But it would be a world where you couldn't cause suffering without first understanding, in your own skin, what you were asking someone else to bear.
